caption: What if you could tickle yourself? Try it: tickle your own foot and almost nothing happens. That's because your cerebellum predicts the touch your own hand is about to make, and your brain turns the feeling down. When someone else tickles you, your brain can't predict it, so it tickles. In 1999, scientists at University College London had people tickle their own palm through a robot arm. When the robot added a delay, the touch felt more and more tickly, up to 0.2 seconds. There are even two kinds of tickle: a light, crawly one called knismesis and the laugh-out-loud one called gargalesis. And it's not just us: rats laugh when tickled, with 50 kHz squeaks far too high for human ears, and they even jump for joy. Where are YOU most ticklish? 👇
